## Introduction

The [Poverty and Inequality Platform (PIP)](https://pip.worldbank.org/) is the World Bank's primary tool for measuring global poverty. `pip_GPT` is a Shiny chatbot that lets analysts query PIP data in plain English — asking questions like *"What was India's headcount poverty rate at $2.15 in 2019?"* and getting a direct, data-backed answer.

Building a conversational interface over an internal dataset is straightforward enough. The more interesting challenge is the AI backend: **standard OpenAI API calls are not permitted from inside the World Bank's network.** Instead, the Bank provides an internal gateway called the **mAI Factory** — an Azure API Management (APIM) layer that proxies Azure OpenAI deployments, enforces access controls, and adds required audit headers.

This post documents the integration pattern so other World Bank developers can replicate it in their own R/Shiny projects. The key moving parts are:

1. Acquiring an Azure AD Bearer token via Posit Connect's OAuth integration
2. Structuring HTTP requests for the mAI Factory endpoint
3. Routing user questions through a two-stage classifier before calling the LLM

---

## What is World Bank mAI Factory?

The mAI Factory exposes Azure OpenAI deployments (including `gpt-4o-mini`, `gpt-4o`, etc.) behind Azure API Management. Developers never call OpenAI's public endpoints; instead they call internal APIM endpoints, authenticated with an Azure AD Bearer token.

Three environments are available:

```r
API_BASE_URLS <- list(
  DEV  = "https://azapimdev.worldbank.org/conversationalai/v2/openai/deployments",
  QA   = "https://azapimqa.worldbank.org/conversationalai/v2/openai/deployments",
  PROD = "https://azapim.worldbank.org/conversationalai/v2/openai/deployments"
)
```

The URL structure mirrors the [Azure OpenAI REST API](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-services/openai/reference):

```
{base_url}/{model}/chat/completions?api-version={version}
```

So a call to `gpt-4o-mini` on DEV resolves to:

```
https://azapimdev.worldbank.org/conversationalai/v2/openai/deployments/gpt-4o-mini/chat/completions?api-version=2025-01-01-preview
```

This means any code already targeting the Azure OpenAI API can be pointed at the mAI Factory with minimal changes — you only swap the base URL and switch from an `api-key` header to a Bearer token.

---

## Authentication: Azure AD via Posit Connect OAuth

This is the part that trips most developers up. You cannot interactively log in to Azure AD from a headless Shiny app. The solution is to delegate credential acquisition to **Posit Connect**, which maintains an OAuth integration with the World Bank's Azure AD tenant.

### How it works

When `pip_GPT` is deployed on the internal Posit Connect server, Connect can exchange credentials on behalf of the running content. The `connectapi` package exposes this via `get_oauth_content_credentials()`, which takes an `audience` argument — the GUID of the registered OAuth integration for mAI.

```r
OAUTH_INTEGRATION_GUID <- "20c434c5-78f1-431f-a286-76980748bc93"

get_azure_token <- function() {
  connect_server  <- "https://datanalytics-int.worldbank.org/"
  connect_api_key <- Sys.getenv('API_KEY') # Posit Connect API key set as env var

  if (connect_server == "" || connect_api_key == "") {
    stop("This app must run on Posit Connect. CONNECT_SERVER / CONNECT_API_KEY not set.")
  }

  client      <- connectapi::connect(server = connect_server, api_key = connect_api_key)
  credentials <- connectapi::get_oauth_content_credentials(
    connect  = client,
    audience = OAUTH_INTEGRATION_GUID
  )
  credentials$access_token
}
```

The returned `access_token` is a short-lived Azure AD Bearer token that can be used in the `Authorization` header of any mAI Factory request.

### Reactive token in the Shiny server

Because the token is tied to the user session, `pip_GPT` retrieves it once per session using a Shiny `reactive()`:

```r
azure_token <- shiny::reactive({
  tryCatch(
    get_azure_token(),
    error = function(e) {
      shiny::showNotification(paste("Token error:", e$message), type = "error")
      NULL
    }
  )
})
```

Any handler that calls the LLM simply calls `azure_token()` to get a valid token, and Shiny's reactivity ensures the retrieval runs at most once per session.

### Prerequisites for replication

To use this pattern in your own app you need:

- The app deployed on the internal Posit Connect instance (`datanalytics-int.worldbank.org`)
- `API_KEY` set as a Posit Connect environment variable (the Connect API key, not an OpenAI key)
- The `OAUTH_INTEGRATION_GUID` for the mAI integration — add the mAI OAuth integration on `datanalytics-int.worldbank.org`; the GUID is auto-generated and can be copied from there

---

## Making the API Call

With a valid token in hand, calling the mAI Factory looks nearly identical to a standard OpenAI chat completions call. The differences are the endpoint URL, the Bearer token in the `Authorization` header, and two extra audit headers (`x-source-type` and `x-team-name`) that mAI requires.

```r
API_VERSION     <- "2025-01-01-preview"
REQUEST_TIMEOUT <- 120
DEFAULT_MODEL   <- "gpt-4o-mini"

openai_chat_response <- function(prompt, token, model = DEFAULT_MODEL) {
  api_url <- paste0(API_BASE_URLS$DEV, "/", model, "/chat/completions")

  headers <- c(
    "Authorization" = paste("Bearer", token),
    "x-source-type" = "interactive",
    "x-team-name"   = "pip",
    "Content-Type"  = "application/json"
  )

  payload <- list(
    messages   = list(list(role = "user", content = prompt)),
    max_tokens = 1000
  )

  response <- httr::POST(
    url    = api_url,
    query  = list(`api-version` = API_VERSION),
    httr::add_headers(.headers = headers),
    body   = payload,
    encode = "json",
    httr::timeout(REQUEST_TIMEOUT)
  )

  if (httr::http_status(response)$category != "Success") {
    stop("mAI Factory API error: ", httr::status_code(response), " - ",
         httr::content(response, "text", encoding = "UTF-8"))
  }

  parsed <- httr::content(response, "parsed", "application/json")
  parsed$choices[[1]]$message$content
}
```

A few design decisions worth noting:

- **`x-team-name: pip`** — mAI uses this for usage attribution. Set it to your team's identifier.
- **`x-source-type: interactive`** — signals that the call is user-driven, as opposed to a batch job.
- **120-second timeout** — LLM responses can be slow, especially for longer prompts. The default `httr` timeout is too short.
- **Response extraction** follows the standard Azure OpenAI JSON structure: `choices[[1]]$message$content`.

## A Two-Stage Query Classifier

`pip_GPT` handles two types of questions: those about PIP poverty data, and everything else. This distinction matters because data questions require several extra LLM calls (parameter extraction, result summarisation) and a database lookup, whereas general questions can be answered directly.

A naive approach would be to send every question to the LLM with a classification prompt. This adds latency and token cost to every interaction — including simple greetings or general knowledge questions. Instead, `pip_GPT` uses a **two-stage classifier** that avoids LLM calls whenever possible.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A([User sends question]) --> B{Stage 1<br/>Keyword check}
    B -->|Match found| C[is_data_query = yes]
    B -->|No match| D[Stage 2<br/>LLM classifier]
    D -->|yes| C
    D -->|no| E[is_data_query = no]
    C --> F[Extract params via LLM<br/>Fetch & filter data<br/>Optional: build plot<br/>Summarise via LLM]
    E --> G[Direct LLM answer]
    F --> H([Display response])
    G --> H
```

### Stage 1: Fast keyword detection (zero LLM cost)

`is_data_keyword()` uses regex to detect poverty-domain signals in the question. If any pattern matches, the question is classified as a data query immediately — no API call needed.

```r
is_data_keyword <- function(question) {
  # Core PIP / poverty-domain keywords
  pip_keywords <- c(
    "PIP",                        # explicit PIP data reference
    "poverty line",
    "poverty gap",
    "poverty rate",
    "poverty data",
    "headcount",
    "welfare",
    "povline",
    "\\$\\s*\\d",                 # dollar poverty lines: $2.15, $3.65 etc.
    "\\d+\\.?\\d*\\s*(usd|\\$)", # amount + USD/$ anywhere
    "gini",
    "inequality",
    "mean consumption",
    "mean income",
    "income distribution",
    "consumption distribution",
    "reporting level",
    "welfare type",
    "fill.?gaps",
    "nowcast",
    "\\bget_stats\\b",
    "\\bpipapi\\b",
    "\\bpip\\b"                   # standalone "pip" (case-insensitive below)
  )

  any(grepl(
    paste(pip_keywords, collapse = "|"),
    question,
    ignore.case = TRUE,
    perl = TRUE
  ))
}
```

### Stage 2: LLM binary classification (only when keywords are inconclusive)

For questions that slip past keyword detection — e.g. *"How poor is Sub-Saharan Africa compared to South Asia?"* — a second stage sends the question to the LLM with a carefully constrained prompt. The prompt provides the full data dictionary and `get_stats()` function signature as context, and strictly requires a single-word `yes` or `no` response.

```r
build_classify_prompt <- function(dict_text, get_stats_args, user_question) {
  paste0(
    "You are a classifier. Your only job is to answer 'yes' or 'no'.\n",
    "Answer 'yes' if the question asks about ANY of the following:\n",
    "  - PIP data, poverty data, or World Bank poverty statistics\n",
    "  - Variables in the poverty dataset listed below\n",
    "  - Arguments to the get_stats function listed below\n",
    "  - Country-level poverty, welfare, inequality, or consumption data\n",
    "  - Headcount ratios, poverty gaps, poverty lines (e.g. $2.15, $3.65)\n",
    "  - Gini coefficients, mean income, mean consumption\n",
    "  - Any question naming a specific country AND a poverty-related concept\n",
    "  - Trends, comparisons, or time-series of the above\n",
    "Answer 'no' for all other questions (weather, sports, general knowledge, etc.).\n",
    "Respond with ONLY the single word 'yes' or 'no'. No explanation.\n\n",
    "Variables and descriptions:\n",
    dict_text,
    "\n",
    get_stats_args,
    "\nQuestion: ",
    user_question
  )
}
```

Providing the data dictionary as context is important here: without it, the LLM has no way to know that terms like `headcount`, `welfare_type`, or `decile3` are domain-specific and should trigger a `yes`.

### Dispatch in the server

The two stages are wired together in the `observeEvent` handler:

```r
# Stage 1: fast keyword check (no LLM call, zero latency)
keyword_hit <- is_data_keyword(user_question)

if (keyword_hit) {
  is_data_query <- "yes"
} else {
  # Stage 2: LLM classify (only when keywords are inconclusive)
  classify_prompt <- build_classify_prompt(dict_text, get_stats_args, user_question)
  is_data_query   <- tolower(trimws(openai_chat_response(classify_prompt, token)))
}
```

---

## The Full Data Query Pipeline

When `is_data_query == "yes"`, the server runs a four-step pipeline before returning an answer.

### Step 1 — Extract filter parameters from natural language

The LLM is prompted to parse the user's question into a named R list of filter parameters. The prompt includes a country name-to-ISO3 code mapping (180+ countries) to ensure valid codes are returned.

```r
build_param_prompt <- function(country_map, user_question) {
  paste0(
    "Given the following user question, extract only the specified values for the poverty data columns as a named R list. For country_code, use ONLY the valid codes from this mapping: ",
    country_map,
    ". Only include columns that are explicitly mentioned or implied in the question. Only return the R list, no explanation. If the value is empty or NULL don't return them.\n",
    "Columns: country_code, year, reporting_level, welfare_type, region_code, poverty_line.\n",
    "Question: ",
    user_question
  )
}
```

The returned code string is cleaned of any markdown fences and evaluated with `eval(parse(...))`:

```r
param_code_clean <- clean_code(param_code)   # strips ```r ... ``` fences
params <- tryCatch(
  eval(parse(text = param_code_clean)),
  error = function(e) list()
)
```

### Step 2 — Fetch and filter local data

Poverty data is pre-cached in FST format (`data/pov_3.fst`), a binary columnar format that loads ~10x faster than CSV. The extracted parameters are applied as successive `dplyr::filter()` calls:

```r
pov_data <- get_poverty_data(povline)   # reads FST cache

filtered <- pov_data
for (nm in names(params)) {
  if (nm != "poverty_line") {
    filtered <- dplyr::filter(filtered, .data[[nm]] %in% params[[nm]])
  }
}
```

### Step 3 — Generate a plot (optional)

If the question contains plot-related keywords (`"plot"`, `"visualize"`, `"chart"`, `"trend"`, etc.), a `ggplot2` chart is built automatically. `build_chat_plot()` infers the y-axis variable by scoring each column's dictionary description against the words in the user's question, then falls back to a priority list (`headcount` > `poverty_gap` > `pop` > `mean` > `gini`) if no strong match is found. When multiple countries are present in the filtered data, the chart colours by country.

### Step 4 — Summarise the result in plain language

The filtered data is serialised to JSON and sent back to the LLM with a final extraction prompt:

```r
build_extract_prompt <- function(user_question, result_json) {
  paste0(
    "Given the following user question and the filtered data in JSON format, extract and present only the relevant information that answers the question.\n",
    "User question: ",
    user_question,
    "\n",
    "Filtered data (JSON): ",
    result_json,
    "\nRespond concisely."
  )
}
```

The LLM's plain-language answer is rendered as markdown in the chat UI.

---

## Key Takeaways and Replication Notes

The integration pattern used in `pip_GPT` can be summarised as:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[Shiny app<br/>on Posit Connect] -->|connectapi OAuth| B[Azure AD<br/>Bearer token]
    B -->|Authorization: Bearer| C[mAI Factory APIM<br/>azapim*.worldbank.org]
    C -->|Azure OpenAI API| D[GPT-4o-mini<br/>deployment]
```

To replicate this in your own R Shiny project:

| Requirement | Detail |
|---|---|
| Posit Connect deployment | App must run on the internal Connect server (`datanalytics-int.worldbank.org`) |
| `API_KEY` env var | Your Posit Connect API key, set in the app's environment variables on Connect |
| OAuth integration GUID | Add the mAI OAuth integration on `datanalytics-int.worldbank.org`; the GUID is auto-generated when the integration is added and can be copied from there |
| `x-team-name` header | Set to your team's identifier for usage attribution |
| Environment choice | Start with DEV; graduate to QA/PROD when ready for production traffic |

The `connectapi` and `httr` packages are the only non-standard dependencies for the integration itself. The rest of the stack — Shiny, `dplyr`, `ggplot2` — is standard R.

One aspect worth emphasising for prompt engineering: **always provide domain context in classification prompts.** In `pip_GPT`, the full data dictionary is injected into the classifier prompt. Without it, the LLM cannot reliably distinguish `"What is India's headcount?"` (a data query) from `"What is a headcount?"` (a general question). The more precisely you define the boundaries of your domain, the more reliably the classifier performs.
